title: Choose Informative Questions
outcome: By the end, I can choose a question that separates possibilities rather than repeating a constant clue.
scenario: A fictional guessing game has eight catalogue cards and asks yes/no questions to narrow the target.
given: Cards: four mystery, four science; six paperback, two hardback; all English.
Compare worst-case remaining group size after asking mystery?, paperback? or English?. No claim about unequal target probabilities is made.

steps.label: List possibilities
steps.detail: There are eight possible target cards initially.

steps.label: Mystery question
steps.detail: Yes group 4; No group 4; largest remaining group 4.

explanation: Under the stated worst-case criterion, mystery is the most useful of these questions because it leaves at most four cards. The constant language clue never narrows the set. This is an identification-game criterion; a classifier fitting labels may instead compare prediction errors or another declared training measure.

counterfactual.change: The current possibility set contains only the four mystery cards.
counterfactual.prediction: Asking mystery now leaves all four; it no longer narrows the set.
counterfactual.reason: Question value depends on the remaining candidates, not just on its wording.

student_task: Choose the best original question and explain why its more balanced split matters here.
teacher_answer: Mystery gives 4/4 and worst case 4, better than paperback’s 6 and English’s 8 under the declared smallest-worst-case rule.
project_evidence: Choose recommender questions that distinguish feasible options, documenting the decision criterion rather than asking unnecessary personal details.
limits: Balanced groups do not guarantee a truthful user answer or optimal choices under every probability or cost model.
review_note: New fictional case individually matched to this topic, with computations and policy traces checked. Use for supported practice; preserve the independent assessment.
